classification_signals: The paper introduces 'identity campaigning' as a third approach to environmental challenges (p. 10, 13). It synthesizes existing psychological and social science research to build a case for this new approach and propose strategies (p. 14-15). It does not present new empirical data but rather draws on a wide range of cited empirical studies to support its theoretical propositions. The authors are a Change Strategist at WWF-UK and a Professor of Psychology, indicating a blend of practical strategy and academic grounding.
title: Meeting Environmental Challenges: The Role of Human Identity

findings.antecedent: strong endorsement of self-enhancing, materialistic values (power, achievement, financial success, popularity, image, status)
findings.consequent: negative attitudes towards non-human nature
findings.source: p. 18, Schultz et al., 2005; Saunders and Munro, 2000; Good, 2007
findings.quote: people who strongly endorse such self-enhancing, materialistic values also express more negative attitudes towards non-human nature.

findings.antecedent: stronger values placed on power and achievement
findings.consequent: concern about how environmental damage affects other humans, children, future generations and non-human life
findings.quote: stronger values placed on power and achievement are associated with less concern about how environmental damage affects other humans, children, future generations and non-human life.

findings.antecedent: self-enhancing values promoting concern about ecological damage
findings.consequent: concern about ecological damage
findings.quote: this concern is limited to an egotistic consideration of how such damage might affect one personally.

findings.antecedent: stronger endorsement of materialistic goals in life (adolescents)
findings.consequent: engagement in positive environmental behaviours (e.g., turning off lights, recycling, reusing paper)
findings.quote: adolescents who more strongly endorse materialistic goals in life report themselves as being less likely to turn off lights in unused rooms, to recycle, to reuse paper

findings.antecedent: materialistic values (American adults)
findings.consequent: frequency of engagement in pro-environmental behaviours (e.g., riding a bicycle, reusing paper, buying second-hand, recycling)
findings.quote: materialistic values are found to be negatively correlated with the frequency of engagement in pro-environmental behaviours

findings.antecedent: high focus on materialistic goals
findings.consequent: ecological footprint arising from lifestyle choices (transportation, housing, diet)
findings.quote: A relatively high focus on materialistic goals related to a higher ecological footprint arising from lifestyle choices regarding transportation, housing and diet.

findings.antecedent: group composition of individuals with relatively high materialistic goals (forest-management game)
findings.consequent: exploitation of forest resources
findings.quote: groups composed of four individuals who all scored relatively highly in materialistic goals exploited the forest resources more intensively

findings.antecedent: citizens placing greater priority on pursuing goals such as wealth, achievement and status (national level)
findings.consequent: per capita CO2 emissions
findings.quote: per capita CO2 emissions were higher in countries where citizens placed a greater priority on pursuing goals such as wealth, achievement and status.

findings.antecedent: people's in-group/out-group classification of others
findings.consequent: treatment of members of these groups
findings.source: p. 20, Hewstone et al., 2002; Whitley & Kite, 2006
findings.quote: people typically treat members of these groups in ways that enhance the standing of their in-group relative to the out-group

findings.antecedent: experiences of environmental identity and relationship with the natural world
findings.consequent: pro-environmental behaviours
findings.quote: a relationship with the natural world fosters pro-environmental behaviours.

findings.antecedent: connectedness with nature
findings.consequent: environmental attitudes and behaviours
findings.source: p. 21, Frantz et al., 2005; Mayer & Frantz, 2004; Schultz, 2001
findings.quote: connectedness is strongly correlated with environmental attitudes and behaviours

findings.antecedent: tendency to define humans as an in-group (anthropocentrism) and perceived split between humans and non-human nature
findings.consequent: indifference to the suffering of individual non-human animals and destruction of the non-human natural world
findings.quote: The tendency to define humans as an in-group is called anthropocentrism... it leads to a heightened indifference to the suffering of both individual non-human animals and the destruction of the non-human natural world

findings.antecedent: describing an individual in nonhuman terms
findings.consequent: perception that the individual is 'not one of us' and not a bona fide member of one's own human group
findings.quote: describing an individual in nonhuman terms implies that the individual is 'not one of us'

findings.antecedent: use of animal nouns in a derogatory way to deprecate human out-groups
findings.consequent: prejudice against animals as an out-group themselves
findings.quote: The use of animal nouns in a derogatory way, to deprecate human out-groups, also belies a prejudice against animals as an out-group themselves.

findings.antecedent: people's belief that only humans experience 'secondary emotions' (e.g., remorse, affection, pride, conceit)
findings.consequent: denial of humanness to out-group members (by presuming lower emotional development)
findings.quote: people denied out-group members some level of humanness by presuming that they shared a lower level of emotional development, comparable to that of non-human animals.

findings.antecedent: ascribing greater rights to individual animals
findings.consequent: positive orientations toward the environment
findings.quote: those who ascribe greater rights to individual animals also express more positive orientations toward the environment.

findings.antecedent: tendency to define non-human nature as an out-group
findings.consequent: emergence of a stronger connection to nature and likelihood of pro-environmental behaviour
findings.quote: The tendency to define non-human nature as an out-group will frustrate the emergence of a stronger connection to nature, and thus undermine the likelihood that people will engage in more pro-environmental behaviour.

findings.antecedent: awareness of the scale of environmental problems
findings.consequent: sense of threat (scared, anxious, guilt, threats to self-esteem/identity)
findings.quote: awareness of the scale of environmental problems that humans confront can lead people to experience a sense of threat.

findings.antecedent: thoughts of global warming creating feelings of fear or helplessness
findings.consequent: distraction strategies (limiting exposure to information, keeping thoughts in the present, doing something small)
findings.quote: people distracted themselves when thoughts of global warming created feelings of fear or helplessness

findings.antecedent: seeking pleasure (pursuing exciting experiences/possessions) as a coping strategy for environmental problems
findings.consequent: psychic relief from anxiety and stress from environmental damage
findings.quote: seeking pleasure... seemed to provide psychic relief from anxiety.

findings.antecedent: seeking pleasure as a coping strategy for environmental problems
findings.consequent: positive environmental behaviours
findings.quote: seeking pleasure did not motivate positive environmental behaviours, and in some samples this strategy was actually associated with less engagement in such beneficial behaviours.

findings.antecedent: relativisation (claiming ecological problems are not so great) as a coping strategy
findings.consequent: stress from environmental damage
findings.quote: relativisation... was consistently associated with lower levels of stress from environmental damage

findings.antecedent: endorsing relativisation as a coping strategy
findings.consequent: pro-environmental behaviour
findings.quote: endorsing relativisation did not promote greater pro-environmental behaviour.

findings.antecedent: denial of guilt ('not my fault') as a coping strategy for environmental problems
findings.consequent: stress from environmental problems
findings.source: p. 27, Homburg et al., 2007; Stoll-Kleemann et al., 2001; Norgaard, 2006
findings.quote: denial of guilt helps lower levels of stress from environmental problems

findings.antecedent: denial of guilt as a coping strategy for environmental problems
findings.consequent: positive environmental behaviours
findings.quote: did not propel people to engage in positive environmental behaviours.

findings.antecedent: apathy about environmental problems
findings.consequent: behavioural choices that exacerbate environmental problems
findings.quote: apathy serves to reinforce behavioural choices that exacerbate environmental problems.

findings.antecedent: use of resignation (accepting environmental problems as inevitable) as a coping strategy
findings.consequent: engagement in pro-environmental behaviours
findings.quote: people were significantly less likely to engage in pro-environmental behaviours to the extent that they used the strategy of resignation

findings.antecedent: brief reminders of one's own mortality
findings.consequent: appeal of materialistic values
findings.source: p. 29, Kosloff & Greenberg, 2009; Sheldon & Kasser, 2008; Solomon & Arndt, 1993; Mandel & Heine, 1999; Kasser & Sheldon, 2000
findings.quote: brief thoughts of one's own death can increase the appeal of materialistic values

findings.antecedent: thinking about death
findings.consequent: antagonism towards out-group members
findings.quote: thinking about death leads judges to assign harsher punishments to prostitutes, Americans to provide greater monetary rewards to those who uphold common cultural values, and college students to be more antagonistic towards out-group members

findings.antecedent: writing about one's own death
findings.consequent: disgust by animals (maggots, cockroaches) and body products
findings.quote: subjects who had written about their own death became especially disgusted by animals (seeing maggots or cockroaches) and body products

findings.antecedent: writing about one's own death
findings.consequent: negative attitudes towards authors proclaiming similarities between animals and humans
findings.quote: subjects who had written about their own death rated the author of the essay proclaiming the similarities between animals and humans as less likable, intelligent, and knowledgeable than the author who wrote that humans were unique and special.

findings.antecedent: thoughts of death
findings.consequent: negative attitudes towards aspects of human behaviour shared with animals (e.g., breastfeeding, physical aspects of sex) and animals in general
findings.source: p. 30, Goldenberg et al., 2006; Beatson & Halloran, 2007
findings.quote: thoughts of death can cause people to express more negative attitudes towards those aspects of human behaviour that are shared with animals... and towards animals in general

findings.antecedent: thoughts of death
findings.consequent: appreciation of safe, tamed landscape and negative attitudes towards wilderness
findings.quote: thoughts of death lead many individuals to become more appreciative of a safe, tamed landscape... and to become more negative towards wilderness.

findings.antecedent: writing about death (vs. listening to music)
findings.consequent: bids to cut down acres of forest (in a simulated timber company task)
findings.quote: Subjects who had written about death made bids to cut down significantly more acres of forest.

findings.antecedent: environmental campaign tactics reinforcing environmentally problematic aspects of identity (e.g., self-enhancing, materialistic values, in-group/out-group distinctions, maladaptive coping)
findings.consequent: environmental problems
findings.quote: Such campaigns, therefore, may exacerbate environmental problems in the longer term because they promote those very features of human identity that contribute to environmental degradation.

findings.antecedent: exposure to messages promoting materialistic values
findings.consequent: adoption of materialistic values
findings.quote: exposing people to messages promoting materialistic values tends to lead them to adopt such values themselves.

findings.antecedent: psychological insecurity (e.g., reminders of death, emotionally cold/controlling parents, childhood divorce, economic deprivation, temporary hunger)
findings.consequent: orientation towards materialistic values
findings.quote: Psychological insecurity is the second factor known to cause an orientation towards materialistic values.

findings.antecedent: prioritization of intrinsic goals (self-acceptance, affiliation, community feeling)
findings.consequent: prioritization of extrinsic/materialistic goals
findings.quote: Intrinsic goals... tend to be antagonistic to the extrinsic goals: it is psychologically difficult for individuals to pursue both intrinsic and extrinsic goals simultaneously.

findings.antecedent: prioritization of values such as self-acceptance/self-direction, affiliation/benevolence, and community feeling/universalism
findings.consequent: environmentally damaging self-enhancing and materialistic values
findings.quote: such values both oppose environmentally damaging self-enhancing and materialistic values and promote more positive environmental attitudes and sustainable lifestyles

findings.antecedent: environmental campaigns appealing to selfish desires and economic benefits of environmental goals
findings.consequent: reinforcement of self-enhancing, materialistic values and perception of nature as an economic resource
findings.quote: the environmental movement serves to reinforce the self-enhancing, materialistic values that... are associated with more environmentally destructive behaviours.

findings.antecedent: framing a recycling task as relevant to the intrinsic goal of benefiting the community (vs. materialistic goal of saving money)
findings.consequent: deeper learning of material and voluntary engagement in recycling-related activities (e.g., visiting library/recycling plant)
findings.quote: those who had the goal framed in intrinsic terms not only learned the material in the text more deeply, but were also more likely to voluntarily visit the library and a recycling plant to learn more about recycling.

findings.antecedent: advertisements and marketing
findings.consequent: encouragement of self-enhancing, materialistic values
findings.quote: advertisements and marketing are prominent means by which self-enhancing, materialistic values are encouraged.

findings.antecedent: use of national performance measures based on financial transactions (e.g., GDP, stock market indices, consumer confidence)
findings.consequent: reinforcement of materialistic goals
findings.quote: It seems highly likely that the use of such measures tends to reinforce materialistic goals

findings.antecedent: adoption and reporting of alternative national progress indicators (including non-materialistic values)
findings.consequent: messages about national priorities received by policymakers and citizens
findings.quote: policy makers and citizens would receive a fundamentally different set of messages about national priorities.

findings.antecedent: environmental organisations discussing and developing policies that enhance intrinsic and self-transcendent values
findings.consequent: legitimisation of intrinsic and self-transcendent values in public discourse and promotion of positive environmental attitudes and behaviours
findings.quote: intrinsic and self-transcendent values will become more legitimised in public discourse. As we have shown above, this, in turn, can be expected to promote more positive environmental attitudes and behaviours.

findings.antecedent: individuals holding more intrinsic and self-transcendent values
findings.consequent: engagement in pro-environmental behaviour
findings.quote: individuals who hold more intrinsic and self-transcendent values are more likely to engage in pro-environmental behaviour.

findings.antecedent: social support
findings.consequent: psychological stress
findings.quote: social support is an important buffer against psychological stress

findings.antecedent: choosing to 'downshift' or pursue a 'voluntarily simple' lifestyle
findings.consequent: ecologically sustainable ways of living
findings.quote: those who have chosen to ‘downshift' or pursue a 'voluntarily simple' lifestyle also live in more ecologically sustainable ways

findings.antecedent: developing concrete 'if-then' implementation intentions
findings.consequent: likelihood of behaving in ways consistent with stated goals
findings.quote: people are more likely to behave in ways consistent with their stated goals when they have previously developed a very concrete if-then statement

findings.antecedent: environmental organisations inadvertently exacerbating in-group/out-group distinctions between humans and nature
findings.consequent: undermining campaigns to motivate pro-environmental behaviour
findings.quote: some environmental organisations may inadvertently exacerbate in-group/out-group distinctions between humans and nature, thereby undermining campaigns

findings.antecedent: environmental organisations dismissing opposition to culling wild animals
findings.consequent: public opposition to clear felling old-growth forests
findings.quote: when environmental organisations dismiss opposition to culling wild animals, this will weaken public opposition to, for example, clear felling old-growth forests.

findings.antecedent: depreciating the value of individual animals
findings.consequent: perceived distinction between humans and non-human animals
findings.quote: depreciating the value of individual animals may tend to exacerbate the perceived distinction between humans and non-human animals

findings.antecedent: conservation activities framing natural world as separate from humans or reinforcing an instrumentalist view of nature
findings.consequent: perception that humans are separate from nature
findings.quote: The perception that humans are separate from nature is likely to be heightened both by conservation activities that frame the natural world as something that does not include humans

findings.antecedent: individuals high in Social Dominance Orientation (SDO)
findings.consequent: negative attitudes towards a wide range of out-groups (races, sexes, sexual orientations, castes, political groups)
findings.quote: individuals high in SDO express more negative attitudes towards a wide range of out-groups

findings.antecedent: college students displaying higher levels of SDO
findings.consequent: endorsement and personal use of “products made by injuring or killing animals”
findings.quote: college students displaying higher levels of SDO are significantly more likely to endorse and personally use “products made by injuring or killing animals”

findings.antecedent: empathy ('other-oriented emotional response congruent with another's perceived welfare')
findings.consequent: prejudicial attitudes towards out-group members
findings.source: p. 51, Batson et al., 1997; Whitley & Kite, 2006
findings.quote: empathy... is consistently associated with lower levels of prejudicial attitudes towards a variety of out-group members.

findings.antecedent: high empathy
findings.consequent: materialistic values
findings.quote: People high in empathy tend to be low in materialistic values and high in intrinsic values

findings.antecedent: egalitarian values (priority on treating others equally)
findings.consequent: prejudice
findings.quote: egalitarian values... has even been called “the prejudice antidote”

findings.antecedent: activation of egalitarian values and empathy
findings.consequent: prejudice and discrimination against human out-groups
findings.quote: prejudice and discrimination against human out-groups decline when egalitarian values and empathy are activated in people's minds.

findings.antecedent: value confrontation (feedback on discrepancies between egalitarian values and behaviour/peers' values)
findings.consequent: alignment of values and behaviour
findings.quote: seems to create an uncomfortable emotional state to which individuals respond by attempting to bring their values and behaviour into alignment.

findings.antecedent: perspective-taking (imagining how animals in harmful situations feel)
findings.consequent: biospheric environmental concern (concern for all living things)
findings.quote: Subjects who were asked to take the animals' perspective were found to express significantly higher levels of biospheric environmental concern

findings.antecedent: contact between human groups (under certain conditions)
findings.consequent: anxiety associated with meeting others different from oneself, empathy for out-group members, re-categorisation into a 'we' identity
findings.quote: contact can reduce the anxiety associated with meeting others different from oneself, create empathy for out-group members, and lead people to re-categorise in-groups and out-groups into a ‘we' identity

findings.antecedent: direct experience of the outdoors
findings.consequent: therapeutic value (for individuals, particularly children)
findings.quote: many studies identify direct experience of the outdoors as having therapeutic value

findings.antecedent: environmental organisations bemoaning public apathy or admonishing individuals for coping mechanisms
findings.consequent: resistance to positive behaviour change
findings.quote: Because such approaches are themselves threatening, they are likely to increase resistance to positive behaviour change

findings.antecedent: reporting unpleasant emotions (anger, sadness) in response to environmental stresses
findings.consequent: engagement in positive environmental behaviours
findings.quote: those subjects who report unpleasant emotions such as anger and sadness in response to environmental stresses are more likely to engage in positive environmental behaviours.

findings.antecedent: sustained, reflective meditation on feelings aroused by thoughts of death
findings.consequent: materialistic strivings
findings.source: p. 58, Cozzolino et al., 2004; Lykins et al., 2007
findings.quote: a more sustained, reflective meditation on the feelings aroused by thoughts of death can actually decrease materialistic strivings

findings.antecedent: brief reminders of one's own death
findings.consequent: suppression of associated thoughts and emotions
findings.source: p. 58, Arndt et al., 2004; Kosloff & Greenberg, 2009
findings.quote: when people are reminded of their own death, they quickly suppress the associated thoughts and emotions

findings.antecedent: provision of an alternative means of coping with fear of death (e.g., thinking about possibility of an afterlife)
findings.consequent: unsustainable exploitation of simulated natural resources (effect of mortality salience)
findings.quote: this effect disappeared when people were provided with an alternative means of coping with the fear of their own death

findings.antecedent: endorsing problem-solving coping strategy
findings.consequent: engagement in positive environmental behaviours
findings.quote: one of the best predictors of engaging in positive environmental behaviours was endorsing this problem-solving coping strategy.

findings.antecedent: problem-solving coping strategies for environmental challenges
findings.consequent: reported stress from awareness of environmental challenges
findings.quote: problem-solving... was associated with increased levels of reported stress from an awareness of environmental challenges.

findings.antecedent: cultivation of mindfulness
findings.consequent: desire for materialistic attainments
findings.quote: mindfulness was associated with reduced desire for materialistic attainments

findings.antecedent: more mindful people
findings.consequent: endorsement of materialistic values
findings.quote: more mindful people were less likely to endorse materialistic values and more likely to endorse intrinsic values.

findings.antecedent: more mindful adults
findings.consequent: positive environmental behaviours and lower ecological footprints
findings.quote: adults who were more mindful engaged in more positive environmental behaviours and had lower ecological footprints

findings.antecedent: highlighting the scale and finality (or irreparability) of an environmental threat
findings.consequent: counterproductive effects (e.g., increasing mortality awareness)
findings.quote: Highlighting the scale and finality (or irreparability) of an environmental threat may therefore be counterproductive.

findings.antecedent: environmental communications exaggerating impact of simple/painless steps
findings.consequent: individuals deploying diversion strategies (less inclined to adopt difficult behavioural changes)
findings.quote: communications which exaggerate the environmental impact of simple and painless steps might actually serve to encourage individuals to deploy such strategies for diversion

findings.antecedent: environmental campaigns blaming other social groups or nationalities
findings.consequent: sense of threat for targeted individuals and likelihood of deploying environmentally problematic coping strategies; projection of guilt onto other groups for non-targeted individuals
findings.quote: such campaigns might: (i) increase the sense of threat of those individuals who are targeted... and (ii) lead those who do not belong to the groups that are singled out to engage in projection

findings.antecedent: vilifying SUV drivers (campaign)
findings.consequent: denial of guilt by drivers of smaller cars and projection of guilt onto SUV drivers; overall traffic-related emissions
findings.quote: vilifying SUV drivers may promote denial of the guilt that drivers of smaller cars could otherwise feel, by encouraging projection of this guilt onto SUV drivers. As such, the campaign could have served to increase overall traffic-related emissions.

findings.antecedent: most aspects of human identity
findings.consequent: shaping by genetic and cultural factors
findings.quote: most aspects of human identity (and the human psyche more broadly) are shaped by both genetic and cultural factors.

findings.antecedent: extent to which people endorse materialistic values
findings.consequent: genetics
findings.source: p. 67, Giddens, et al., 2009; Kasser et al., 2004
findings.quote: the extent to which people endorse materialistic values seems to have little to do with genetics and much more to do with social experiences

findings.antecedent: evaluations attached to categorisations of others
findings.consequent: learning
findings.quote: the evaluations they attach to those categorisations are largely learned

findings.antecedent: means by which people cope with threat
findings.consequent: shaping by messages received from their culture
findings.quote: the means by which people cope with threat is largely shaped by messages received from their culture

findings.antecedent: human brain
findings.consequent: ability to over-ride ultimate programming and substitute other values
findings.quote: the brain - especially the human brain - is well able to over-ride its ultimate programming; well able to dispense with the ultimate value of gene survival and substitute other values.

findings.antecedent: environmental campaigns appealing to self-interested or materialistic values
findings.consequent: short-term and piecemeal behaviour change
findings.quote: Designing campaigns to appeal to existing self-interested or materialistic values may lead to short-term and piecemeal behaviour change

findings.antecedent: environmental campaigns appealing to self-interested or materialistic values
findings.consequent: undermining of more fundamental attempts to address systemic environmental challenges
findings.quote: such an approach runs the risk of undermining more fundamental attempts to address systemic environmental challenges.

findings.antecedent: perceived credibility and trustworthiness of the messenger
findings.consequent: receptivity of an audience to a message
findings.quote: the receptivity of an audience to a message depends largely upon the perceived credibility and trustworthiness of the messenger

findings.antecedent: appeals to environmentally beneficial aspects of people's identity (empathy, egalitarian values)
findings.consequent: public's sense of rapport with environmental organisations and receptivity to environmental campaigns
findings.quote: appeals to the more environmentally beneficial aspects of people's identity... will improve the public's sense of rapport with environmental organisations, and hence their receptivity to environmental campaigns.

findings.antecedent: frames (mental structures)
findings.consequent: ideas, concepts, reasoning, perception, and actions
findings.quote: Frames “structure our ideas and concepts, they shape the way we reason, and they even impact how we perceive and how we act”

findings.antecedent: surface framing (catchy slogans, clever spin)
findings.consequent: effectiveness
findings.quote: Surface framing... cannot work unless these messages resonate with a set of long-term deep frames.

findings.antecedent: social institutions and situations
findings.consequent: frames
findings.quote: our social institutions and situations shape our frames, which in turn shape our institutions.

findings.antecedent: public policy
findings.consequent: predominant frames in society
findings.quote: Public policy, for example, has an important implication for the frames that predominate in society.

findings.antecedent: policy concentrating on material criteria alone
findings.consequent: popularity or instilling long-term values contradicting policy aims
findings.quote: Concentrating on material criteria alone can be counterproductive if a policy is either unpopular, or if it instils in the public's mind long-term values that contradict the aims of the policy

findings.antecedent: campaign (even if unsuccessful in immediate policy terms)
findings.consequent: cognitive impacts (unconsciously responding to deep frames)
findings.quote: even if a campaign is unsuccessful, it will have cognitive impacts – because people will see the campaign materials and unconsciously respond to the deep frames that these enshrine.

findings.antecedent: understanding of cognitive policy
findings.consequent: design of campaign communications that shape deep frames promoting environmental sustainability
findings.quote: Such an understanding can also be used to design campaign communications that have a widespread positive impact in shaping the deep frames that promote environmental sustainability

findings.antecedent: values and aspects of identity frustrating systemic responses to environmental challenges
findings.consequent: values and identities frustrating delivery on other challenges (war, aggression, poverty, racism, homophobia, sexism, prejudice against disabled, human rights abuse, indifference to animal welfare)
findings.quote: there is a very high level of coincidence between the values and aspects of identity that currently frustrate systemic responses to environmental challenges and the values and identities that frustrate delivery on a range of other challenges

findings.antecedent: self-enhancing, materialistic values
findings.consequent: concern for social justice, equality, world at peace, pro-social behaviour, manipulative/competitive behaviour
findings.quote: self-enhancing, materialistic values are not only associated with more negative environmental attitudes and behaviours, but also with less concern for social justice, equality, and a world at peace, less pro-social behaviour, and more manipulative, competitive behaviour

findings.antecedent: maladaptive responses to fear and threats
findings.consequent: problematic environmental behaviour and problematic social behaviours (aggression, victimisation of out-groups)
findings.source: p. 73, Greenberg et al., 2004; Stephan & Stephan, 2000
findings.quote: maladaptive responses to fear and threats not only create a tendency towards problematic environmental behaviour, but also towards a number of other problematic social behaviours

findings.antecedent: exposure to commercial television (children)
findings.consequent: materialistic values
findings.quote: exposure to commercial television increases children's scores on assessments of materialistic values

findings.antecedent: exposure to marketing messages (children)
findings.consequent: problems for young people (alcohol/cigarette use, eating disorders, violence, sexual promiscuity)
findings.quote: exposure to marketing messages is also known to contribute to a host of other problems for young people

limitations: The three aspects of human identity selected for focus do not constitute a complete list, nor are they necessarily the most important features involved in frustrating environmental responses (p. 16).
The application of techniques for reducing prejudice to human-nature relationships is likely to entail specific challenges and requires more work to refine (p. 46).
The proposed agenda extends far beyond the current scope of most environmental organisations, requiring new collaborations (p. 37).
Implementing the proposed approach requires changes in current monitoring and evaluation processes, as success is often defined solely by short-term material policy outcomes (p. 72).
The environmental movement cannot make progress on identity campaigning whilst working alone, necessitating new coalitions (p. 73).
minimum_safe_summary: The paper, "Meeting Environmental Challenges: The Role of Human Identity," proposes "identity campaigning" as a crucial third approach for the environmental movement, alongside engaging organizations and individual behaviors. It synthesizes psychological and social science research to argue that self-enhancing/materialistic values, in-group/out-group distinctions (especially anthropocentrism), and maladaptive coping with fear and threats are environmentally problematic aspects of human identity. Key findings include that materialistic values correlate with negative environmental attitudes and behaviors, anthropocentrism fosters indifference to nature, and common coping strategies for environmental threats (e.g., diversion, denial, apathy, materialistic orientation, out-group denigration) often exacerbate environmental problems. The paper suggests strategies to mitigate these issues by reducing social modeling of materialistic values, promoting intrinsic/self-transcendent values, fostering empathy for non-human nature, and encouraging healthier coping mechanisms like mindfulness and problem-focused action. Limitations include the non-exhaustive nature of the identified identity aspects and the significant challenges in implementing these broad, culturally-focused strategies, often requiring inter-organizational collaboration and changes in evaluation metrics.
